L111: ## Summary
L112: All plants are electrically excitable, but only few are known to fire a well-defined, all-or-nothing action potential (AP). The Venus flytrap Dionaea muscipula displays APs with an extraordinarily high firing frequency and speed, enabling the capture organ of this carnivorous plant to catch small animals as fast as flies. The number of APs triggered by the prey is counted and serves as the basis for decisions within the flytrap's hunting cycle.
L113: The archetypical Dionaea AP lasts 1 s and consists of five phases: Starting from the resting state, an initial cytosolic Ca^{2+} transient is followed by depolarization, repolarization and a transient hyperpolarization (overshoot) before the original membrane potential is finally recovered. When the flytrap matures and becomes excitable, a distinct set of ion channels, pumps and carriers is expressed, each mastering a distinct AP phase.

L123: ## I. Introduction
L124: The Venus flytrap's capability of firing action potentials (APs) is known since Darwin's time from touch-induced membrane potential changes, first monitored by Burdon-Sanderson (cite27†1873 ). Besides Dionaea – according to Charles Darwin – the ‘most wonderful plant of the world’ (Darwin, cite28†1875 ), other actively hunting botanical carnivores also fire APs when in contact with prey (Hedrich & Fukushima, cite29†2021 ).
L125: The flytrap recognizes collisions with living prey or touch by experimenters with the help of trigger hairs emerging from the inner trap surface. These sensory organs are equally spaced, three on each trap lobe (Fig. cite30†1a ). A 3° displacement of a trigger hair by a force of 30 μN – equivalent to the power of a mosquito – is sufficient to provoke an AP (Scherzer et al., cite31†2019 ). The first AP, elicited by the initial touch deflection of a single trigger hair, is memorized for c. 20 s.
L126: If the same or another trigger hair is stimulated within these 20 s to bring a second AP on its way, the trap closes within 0.1 s. Remarkably, a calcium wave travels together and with the same fast speed as the AP (Fig. cite30†1b ). Both signals propagate with up to 10 cm s^{−1} along both trap lobes, a velocity unrivalled by other plant systems.
L127: The cytosolic Ca^{2+} transients of the first and second wave sum up, and upon reaching a critical threshold, they induce the release of viscoelastic energy stored in the open trap, making the trap snap shut (Suda et al., cite32†2020 ). While the entrapped prey tries to escape, it will keep colliding with the trigger hairs and thus sustains AP firing.
L128: After having counted and integrated ‘2’ in the process of AP-dependent trap snapping, the following three to five or more APs are translated into jasmonate (JA) biosynthesis and signalling (Böhm et al., cite33†2016 ).
L129: While the fast trap closure does not require JA, the touch hormone stimulates slow hermetical sealing of the capture organ and the activation of glands that cover the inner surface, which leads to the secretion of digestive enzymes into the newly formed green stomach (Scherzer et al., cite34†2017 ).

L132: cite16†Open in figure viewer cite35†PowerPoint L133: (a) Open Dionaea muscipula trap. Trigger hairs located at the inner trap surface serve as mechanosensors: their displacement provokes the action potential. (b) Upon touch perception, calcium waves and action potentials (APs) are released and together propagate along both trap lobes.
L134: (c) Dionaea's AP consists of five distinct phases: after an initial Ca^{2+} influx via DmGLR3.6, the Ca^{2+} signal is amplified by a Ca^{2+}-induced Ca^{2+} release (CICR) from the endoplasmic reticulum to an all-or-nothing cytosolic Ca^{2+} transient (phase 1). If the Ca^{2+} level passes the threshold, Cl^{−} release via Ca^{2+}-dependent ALMT anion channels triggers an initial, rapid depolarization (phase 2).
L135: Positive of −60 mV, depolarization-dependent DmSKOR K^{+} channels and DmAHA4 H^{+} pumps are activated and slow the depolarization kinetics (1^{st} shoulder). At c. −20 mV, when anion efflux and K^{+} efflux compensate each other, the depolarization maximum is reached. The repolarization (phase 3) sets in when [Ca^{2+}]_{cytosolic} drops, the anion channel inactivates, and DmSKOR and DmAHA4 allow K^{+} and H^{+} release from the cell.
L136: Negative of −60 mV DmSKOR inactivates, slowing the fast, initial repolarization (2^{nd} shoulder). The delayed deactivation of the depolarization-activated H^{+} pump results in sustained H^{+} export, thus provoking a transient overshoot hyperpolarization (phase 4). During membrane hyperpolarization, DmAHA4 voltage inactivates and H^{+}-driven DmHAK5 and NRT-type anion transporters reset the pre-AP resting potential by recharging the K^{+} and anion battery (phase 5).
L137: (d) Two APs drive the cytosolic Ca^{2+} level above the threshold upon which rapid trap closure is unavoidable. Snap buckling is achieved by the release of K^{+} and anions and, in turn, turgor loss in the motor cells of the inner leaflet. As a result, the metastable hydrostatic pressure balance between inner and outer leaflet collapses and the open concave trap geometry flips over to the convex closed one.
L138: The Venus flytrap Dyscalculia (DYSC) mutant cannot properly count and decode the Ca^{2+}-APs and is thus unable to snap close its trap and to produce sufficient JA in response to prolonged mechanostimulation. The JA-dependent steps of the hunting cycle can, however, be rescued by external JA application in DYSC (Iosip et al., cite36†2023 ). This shows that prey capture, recognition and processing are under the control of the Ca^{2+} and the JA clock.
